2500: A capillary is an extremely narrow tube — so narrow that it sits at the boundary of what you can see with the naked eye. The word is used in two main fields: biology (where capillaries are tiny blood vessels) and physics/general science (where a capillary is any tube with a very narrow opening). Both meanings share the same central idea: a tube so thin that remarkable things happen inside it or because of it.
1. Capillary in biology (the most important meaning)

This is the dominant, everyday meaning of the word.

What it is

A capillary is the smallest type of blood vessel in your body. Your body has three kinds of blood vessels:

  • Arteries — thick, muscular tubes that carry blood away from your heart, delivering it outward to the rest of the body.
  • Veins — tubes that carry blood back to the heart.
  • Capillaries — the microscopic, hair-thin tubes that bridge the gap between the arteries and the veins.

Think of it like a city's road system: arteries are the highways, veins are the return roads, and capillaries are the tiny local lanes that weave through every neighbourhood — every organ, muscle, and tissue in your body.

What they look like

Capillaries are almost impossibly small. They are so narrow that red blood cells must pass through them in single file — one by one, not side by side. A single capillary is roughly 5 to 10 micrometres in diameter. (For scale: a human hair is about 70 micrometres wide, so a capillary is many times thinner than a single strand of your hair.)

Their walls are also extraordinarily thin — just one cell thick. That single layer of cells is called the endothelium. No other blood vessel has walls this thin; arteries and veins have several layers of tissue. This thinness is not a weakness — it is the whole point, as you'll see next.

What they do (their function)

Because capillary walls are only one cell thick, substances can pass through those walls very easily in both directions. This is called capillary exchange, and it is one of the most critical processes in your body.

Here is what happens:

  • Oxygen and nutrients (glucose, amino acids, minerals) travel out of the capillary through its thin wall and into the surrounding cells and tissues. Every cell in your body receives its food and oxygen this way.
  • Carbon dioxide and waste products produced by those cells travel into the capillary through the same wall, to be carried away in the blood.

In other words, capillaries are the actual delivery-and-collection points of your body's supply chain. Arteries and veins are just the transport highways; the real work of nourishing your cells and removing their waste happens at the capillary level.

Scale: how many are there?

Capillaries form a vast, dense network throughout virtually every tissue in your body. If you were to lay all the capillaries in one adult human body end to end, they would stretch for roughly 40,000 kilometres — enough to wrap around the Earth at the equator. They are everywhere, because every cell needs to be close to a capillary to receive oxygen and nutrients.

Capillaries and disease

When people talk about "poor circulation," they often mean that blood is not reaching the capillary networks effectively. Conditions like diabetes can damage capillaries over time — particularly in the eyes (causing vision problems), the kidneys (reducing their filtering ability), and the extremities like feet (slowing healing). This is why capillary health matters so much in medicine.

A capillary as a single unit vs. a network

You will encounter the word in both a singular and collective sense:

  • "A capillary" — one individual microscopic tube.
  • "The capillary network" or "capillary bed" — the dense mesh of thousands of these tiny tubes woven through a specific tissue or organ. When blood flows from a small artery into this mesh and then drains into a small vein, that mesh is called a capillary bed.
2. Capillary in physics and general science

Outside of biology, a capillary (also called a capillary tube) refers to any tube — typically made of glass — that has a very small internal diameter.

These tubes are used in laboratories and scientific instruments precisely because of their narrowness, which produces an interesting physical behaviour called capillary action (or capillarity).

What is capillary action?

When you place a narrow capillary tube into a liquid, the liquid does not just sit at the same level inside the tube as it does outside — it either rises up into the tube or gets pushed down, depending on the liquid and the material of the tube. Most commonly, it rises.

This happens because of two competing forces between the liquid molecules and the tube's inner wall:

  • Adhesion: the attraction between liquid molecules and the wall of the tube. This pulls the liquid up along the wall.
  • Cohesion: the attraction between liquid molecules to each other (surface tension). This keeps the liquid surface together.

In a glass capillary tube, water's adhesion to glass is strong, so the water creeps up the inner wall. The narrower the tube, the higher the water climbs. In a wide tube, this effect is barely noticeable. In a very narrow capillary, the water can rise noticeably against gravity.

Why does this matter in real life?

Capillary action is not just a lab curiosity — it is a fundamental mechanism in nature and everyday life:

  • Plants: Trees and plants draw water upward from the soil through their roots and narrow channels in their stems, partly through capillary action. This is how water reaches leaves many metres above the ground, even in the absence of a pump.
  • Paper towels and sponges: When you press a paper towel against a spill, the water is pulled into the tiny gaps and fibres by capillary action.
  • Ink in a pen: Fountain pens and some ballpoint mechanisms rely on capillary action to draw ink toward the tip.
  • Candle wicks: The liquid wax is drawn upward through the wick's fibres by capillary action, feeding the flame.
The single thread connecting both meanings

Whether you are talking about blood vessels in biology or narrow glass tubes in physics, a capillary always refers to something extremely thin and tube-like, and its significance always comes from that thinness. In biology, the thinness enables life-sustaining exchange between blood and cells. In physics, the thinness causes liquids to behave in ways they would not in wider vessels. The narrowness is always the point.

• "The surgeon examined the capillaries at the back of the patient's eye to check for signs of damage."
  • "Nutrients pass from the blood into surrounding tissues through the thin walls of the capillaries."
  • "In the experiment, the researcher dipped a glass capillary into dyed water and watched the liquid rise on its own."
  • "Diabetes can weaken the capillaries in the kidneys over many years."
  • "The dense capillary bed in muscle tissue ensures that every muscle fibre receives a constant supply of oxygen during exercise."
2501:
Capitalism is an economic system in which private individuals or companies — rather than the government — own the resources and tools used to produce goods and services, and where most economic decisions are driven by the pursuit of profit through free markets.

That one sentence is the core.
What Is "Capital"?

The word "capitalism" is built around the concept of capital. Capital isn't just money — it's any asset that can be used to generate more wealth: money, machines, factories, buildings, farmland, technology, vehicles. What makes something "capital" isn't what it is, but what you do with it — you use it to produce things and earn a return.

A simple example: You have ₹50,000 saved up. You use it to buy ingredients, rent a stall, and sell food. After paying your costs, you're left with ₹60,000. That extra ₹10,000 is profit. You've just used capital to generate more capital. In capitalism, this cycle — invest capital → produce → earn profit → reinvest — is the fundamental engine of the whole economy.
Private Ownership: Who Owns What?

In capitalism, the means of production — everything used to make and sell things — are privately owned. This means factories, companies, land, machines, and resources belong to private individuals or private organizations, not to the government or to society as a whole.

Because you privately own these things, you get to decide what to produce, how to produce it, and what to do with the profits. The government doesn't tell you what to make or what price to charge.

This private ownership is what separates capitalism from socialism (where key industries are publicly owned) and communism (where all productive property is collectively owned).
Free Markets and How Prices Are Set

In capitalism, goods and services are exchanged in free markets, and prices are determined by supply and demand — not by government officials.

  • If many people want something that's scarce, its price rises.
  • If something is plentiful but few people want it, its price falls.

This might seem chaotic — who's in charge? The answer is: no one, and that's the point. The economist Adam Smith famously described this as the "invisible hand" — the idea that when millions of individuals and businesses each act in their own self-interest, buying what they want cheaply and selling what they can profitably, the market as a whole tends to allocate resources efficiently, as if guided by an unseen force. No central planner is needed.
The Profit Motive: The Engine of the System

The driving force of capitalism is the desire to earn profit — the money left over after all costs (materials, wages, rent, etc.) are subtracted from revenue.

The profit motive is powerful because it shapes behavior:

  • People start businesses and take risks because they hope to profit.
  • Companies innovate and improve their products to attract more customers and earn more.
  • Inefficiency is punished — if your costs are too high or your product is poor, you lose customers and eventually go out of business.

In capitalism, the profit motive replaces the role that central planning plays in other systems. Rather than a government deciding "we need more steel mills," private investors build steel mills when they see a profit opportunity.
Wage Labor: The Two Main Groups

In capitalism, most people don't own factories or businesses. They own only their own skills and time. So they sell their labor to employers in exchange for a wage or salary.

This creates two broad groups in a capitalist economy:

  1. Capital owners (capitalists): People or companies who own the means of production — factories, businesses, land, machines. They earn profit, rent, and investment returns.
  2. Workers: People who work for wages. They are paid for their time and skills, but they don't own the business and don't receive the profits directly.

This division is one of the most discussed and debated features of capitalism. Owners take risks with their capital and are rewarded when the business succeeds. Workers get stable wages but don't get to share in the upside proportionally.
Competition: Why It Matters

Capitalism depends on competition between businesses. Multiple companies compete for the same customers, and this competition is supposed to benefit everyone:

  • It drives prices down, because a business that charges too much loses customers to cheaper rivals.
  • It drives quality up, because businesses improve their products to attract buyers.
  • It drives innovation, because new ideas and technologies can give a business a competitive edge.
  • It weeds out inefficiency — poorly run businesses fail, and better ones survive.

This is why capitalism is often credited with technological progress. The iPhone, for example, exists partly because tech companies compete fiercely for customers and have a profit incentive to innovate.

However, competition can break down. When one company grows so large that it dominates an industry and faces no real rivals, you get a monopoly. Monopolies can raise prices and stifle innovation because they face no competitive pressure. This is why capitalist governments typically have laws against anti-competitive behavior.
The Role of Government

Purely unregulated capitalism — where the government does absolutely nothing — is called laissez-faire capitalism (meaning "leave it alone"). In this extreme form, there are no labor laws, no consumer protections, no environmental regulations, nothing. The market decides everything.

In practice, no modern country works this way. Every capitalist nation today has a mixed economy — capitalism as the foundation, but with government involvement to:

  • Regulate businesses (e.g., ban monopolies, require safety standards, protect workers)
  • Provide public goods (roads, national defense, basic infrastructure) that markets wouldn't provide well on their own
  • Correct market failures (e.g., taxing pollution, because polluters don't pay for the harm they cause to others)
  • Redistribute wealth to some degree (through taxes, welfare programs, public education, healthcare in some countries)

The degree of government involvement is a spectrum. The United States leans toward less intervention. Scandinavian countries like Sweden and Denmark have capitalism as their economic base but with very strong social safety nets — universal healthcare, free education, generous unemployment benefits. China practices "state capitalism," where the government itself acts as a major business owner while markets operate alongside it.
The Strengths of Capitalism

Capitalism's supporters argue it produces several major benefits:

1. Economic growth and innovation. Historically, capitalism has produced extraordinary increases in living standards and technological progress. The industrial revolution, the digital revolution, and the dramatic reduction in global poverty over the last two centuries are all associated with capitalist economies.

2. Efficiency. Because inefficient businesses lose money and eventually fail, capitalism tends to allocate resources better than systems where the government decides everything.

3. Personal freedom. In capitalism, you're generally free to choose your career, start a business, spend your money as you wish, and pursue your own goals. This economic freedom is often linked to broader political freedom.

4. Decentralization. Rather than relying on one central authority to make all decisions (which is both a massive information problem and a source of corruption), capitalism distributes decision-making across millions of individuals and firms. No single person or government needs to know everything — prices signal information automatically.

5. Responsiveness. Markets respond quickly to changing consumer preferences. If people suddenly want electric cars, companies have an immediate profit incentive to supply them.
The Criticisms of Capitalism

Capitalism has deep and serious critics. Here are the main arguments against it:

1. Inequality. Capitalism naturally tends to concentrate wealth. Those who already own capital earn returns on it automatically — their money makes more money. Those who start with nothing can only earn wages. Over time, this creates and widens the gap between rich and poor. The wealthiest people in a capitalist society become extraordinarily wealthy not just because they worked hard, but because capital itself generates returns.

2. Exploitation of workers. This is the central critique made by Karl Marx. Workers are paid wages, but the goods they produce are sold for more than what they were paid. The difference — what Marx called surplus value — goes to the owner as profit. Workers create value they don't fully receive. Critics argue this is a form of built-in exploitation that defines capitalism.

3. Externalities. When a factory dumps waste into a river to save money, that's a cost imposed on society — polluted water, sick people, dead fish — that doesn't appear in the factory's profit calculation. Capitalism left to itself tends to ignore these "negative externalities." Climate change is the most important modern example: burning fossil fuels is profitable, but the costs (rising temperatures, disasters, displacement) are borne by the whole world.

4. Boom-and-bust cycles. Capitalist economies are prone to cycles of rapid growth followed by crashes, recessions, and mass unemployment. The Great Depression of the 1930s and the global financial crisis of 2008 are stark examples. These cycles cause enormous human suffering.

5. Short-termism. Because companies are often judged by their quarterly profits, they tend to prioritize immediate gains over long-term thinking. This can mean cutting corners on worker safety, depleting natural resources, or investing in what's profitable today rather than sustainable for the future.

6. Power imbalances. Large corporations can become so powerful that they distort the political process in their favor (lobbying, campaign contributions), undermine fair competition, and exploit workers and consumers when people have few other options.

7. Commodification. Critics argue capitalism tends to turn everything — healthcare, education, housing, even art — into a commodity to be bought and sold for profit, even when it might be better treated as a public good that everyone has a right to.
Capitalism vs. Other Economic Systems

To be crystal clear about what capitalism is, it helps to contrast it with the main alternatives:

Feudalism preceded capitalism in medieval Europe. Wealth came from owning land, which was inherited by nobles. Ordinary people (serfs) worked the nobles' land in exchange for protection and had little freedom or opportunity. Capitalism replaced this with a system where wealth comes from commerce and production, class is less rigid (at least in theory), and people can in principle rise by starting businesses.

Socialism argues that key industries and means of production should be owned by the government or the community collectively, so that profits benefit everyone rather than private owners. The goal is greater equality and ensuring production serves social needs. There's a wide range here — from moderate social democracy (like the Nordic model, which is still fundamentally capitalist with a strong welfare state) to more thoroughgoing state ownership of industries.

Communism takes the idea further: all productive property is collectively owned, there are no social classes, and wealth is distributed according to need. In the Marxist vision, this was the endpoint of history. In practice, Communist states (USSR, Maoist China) were characterized by state control of all production and one-party government, with deeply mixed results.

The core difference: capitalism centers private ownership and profit. These alternative systems center collective ownership and social welfare.
The Different Faces of Capitalism

Even within capitalism, there is significant variety in how it operates:

  • Laissez-faire capitalism: Minimal government interference. Markets decide almost everything. (Closest to 19th-century Britain or the US before the 1930s.)
  • Liberal market capitalism: Markets are primary, government regulation is limited, and the social safety net is relatively thin. (The US and UK today lean this way.)
  • Social market capitalism (welfare capitalism): Strong capitalist economy combined with a robust welfare state — universal healthcare, free education, strong worker protections. (Germany, the Nordic countries.)
  • State capitalism: The government owns major companies that compete in markets for profit. (China, Saudi Arabia with Aramco.)
  • Crony capitalism: A distorted form where business success depends more on political connections than on genuine competition or merit. (Common in countries with weak institutions and widespread corruption.)
One Final Summary

Capitalism is an economic system resting on three pillars: (1) private ownership of the resources and businesses that produce goods and services, (2) free markets where prices are set by supply and demand, and (3) the profit motive, which drives decisions about what to produce and how. Most people participate as workers who sell their labor for wages. Competition among businesses is supposed to drive efficiency and innovation. In practice, every capitalist economy today is a mixed economy — private enterprise combined with some level of government regulation and public services — because pure capitalism generates benefits (growth, innovation, freedom) but also serious problems (inequality, exploitation, environmental harm, financial instability) that societies have needed governments to address.
2502: Capitalization is a noun. It has different meanings in different fields. You'll encounter it in writing, in finance, and in accounting.

This is the most common everyday meaning. Capitalization means the practice of using uppercase (capital) letters — and knowing the rules for when to use them.

When you write "Mumbai" instead of "mumbai," or start a sentence with a big letter, you are following the rules of capitalization.

The core rules of capitalization:

The start of every sentence — Every sentence begins with a capital letter.
"She reads every night."

Proper nouns — Names of specific people, places, companies, languages, religions, nationalities, and organizations are always capitalized, because they refer to one particular thing, not a general category.
"Priya," "Delhi," "Google," "Hindi," "Buddhism," "Indian," "the United Nations."
Compare: "I visited a city" (general) vs. "I visited Paris" (specific name).

The word "I" — Always written as a capital letter, wherever it appears in a sentence.

Titles used before a name — "Prime Minister Modi," "Dr. Mehta," "Professor Singh."
But if you use the title without a name, lowercase is usually correct: "The prime minister spoke today."

Days of the week, months, and holidays — "Tuesday," "November," "Eid," "Christmas."
Note: seasons are usually not capitalized — "summer," "winter."

First word inside a direct quotation — She said, "Meet me at five."

Titles of books, films, songs — Major words are capitalized: "The God of Small Things," "Lagaan."

What "bad capitalization" looks like:

If someone writes "i went to mumbai on monday with my friend sita," that is poor capitalization. Correct: "I went to Mumbai on Monday with my friend Sita."

When a teacher or editor says, "Watch your capitalization," they mean you're either missing capital letters where they belong, or using them where they shouldn't be.

This is a completely separate meaning, used in business and investing.

Market capitalization (very commonly shortened to "market cap") means the total value of a company as judged by the stock market.

How it works:

When a company is listed on a stock exchange, its shares are bought and sold every day. The price of one share goes up and down. To find the company's total market value, you multiply:

Market Cap = Price of one share × Total number of shares in existence

Example: Suppose a company called SunTech has 1 crore shares, and each share currently costs ₹200. Then SunTech's market capitalization is ₹200 × 1,00,00,000 = ₹200 crore.

This number answers the question: "What is this entire company worth, according to the stock market, right now?"

Why people care about market cap:

It is the most widely used measure of a company's size. Investors and analysts group companies into categories based on their market cap:

Large-cap companies are big, well-established, generally stable businesses. Examples: Reliance Industries, TCS, Apple, Microsoft. These are considered lower-risk investments.

Mid-cap companies are medium-sized. They have more room to grow, but also more risk than large-caps.

Small-cap companies are smaller businesses. They can grow quickly, but they are also more vulnerable.

When you read news like "Apple's market capitalization crossed $3 trillion," it simply means: if you added up the current price of every single Apple share that exists, the total would be $3 trillion. That's the market's estimate of Apple's worth.

One important thing to note: Market cap reflects what investors think the company is worth, which can change daily as the share price moves. It is not the same as the company's profit, revenue, or the physical value of its buildings and machines.

This is a technical meaning used by accountants and businesses, but the logic behind it is very sensible once you understand it.

Capitalization in accounting means treating a cost as a long-term asset rather than recording it as an immediate expense.

The idea behind it:

When a business spends money, it has to decide how to record that spending. There are two main approaches:

Option A — Expense it immediately: The full cost is recorded as an expense right now, which reduces profit right away.

Option B — Capitalize it: The cost is recorded as an asset on the company's books. The cost is then spread out gradually over the years the asset will be used. This spreading is called depreciation (for physical assets) or amortization (for non-physical assets like software or patents).

When does a company capitalize something?

When the thing being bought will provide value for many years, not just this year. Common examples: buildings, machines, vehicles, computers, and long-term software systems.

Example: A small courier company buys a delivery van for ₹8 lakh. The van will be used for 8 years.

  • If they expense it: ₹8 lakh is deducted from profit this year. Profit looks very low this year, even though the van will be generating income for 8 years.
  • If they capitalize it: The van is recorded as an asset worth ₹8 lakh. Each year, ₹1 lakh is deducted as depreciation. This better reflects reality — the cost is matched to the years during which the van is being used.

So the capitalization of the van refers to the accounting decision to record it as an asset and spread its cost over its useful life.

Why it matters:

This decision affects how a company's profits look on paper. If a company capitalizes too aggressively (records things as assets that should really be expenses), its profits appear inflated. This is why accounting standards and regulators set strict rules about what can and cannot be capitalized.
4. In Business Finance: A Company's Total Capitalization

There is one more sense of the word, also in the business world.

Total capitalization sometimes refers to all the long-term money a company has raised to run and grow its business — whether that money came from investors (equity) or from borrowing (debt).

In other words, it describes how a company is funded.

Example: If a startup raised ₹40 crore by selling shares to investors, and also took a ₹20 crore loan from a bank, its total capitalization is ₹60 crore. This total is the pool of long-term capital it has available.

This usage is closely related to the idea of "capital structure" — the mix of debt and equity a company uses.
The Big Picture: How All the Meanings Connect

At first glance, the word seems to mean very different things. But there is a common thread — in every sense, capitalization involves elevating or enlarging something:

In writing, a small letter is elevated to a large one.

In finance, the market cap elevates a company's individual shares to reflect the total value of the whole company.

In accounting, a single large cost is elevated to the status of a permanent asset, rather than being consumed as a one-time expense.

In business finance, individual sources of funding are combined and elevated into a company's total capital base.

Quick summary in plain words:

If you're talking about writing, capitalization means the rules for using uppercase letters.

If you're talking about the stock market, market capitalization means the total market value of a company (share price multiplied by number of shares).

If you're talking about accounting, capitalization means recording a major purchase as a long-term asset and spreading its cost over time.

If you're talking about how a company is funded, capitalization means the total long-term money a company has raised through shares and loans combined.

The context will almost always make it clear which meaning is intended.
2503:
To capitulate means to stop resisting and give in — but only after you have been resisting for some time.

It describes the moment when someone who has been fighting back, saying no, holding their ground, or refusing to agree... finally breaks down and accepts what they were opposing.

Think of it as the moment resistance ends and surrender begins.
The One Thing That Makes Capitulate Special

This word has one non-negotiable ingredient baked into it: prior resistance.

You cannot capitulate instantly. If someone asks you something and you agree right away, that is not capitulating. But if you pushed back, held firm, argued, refused... and then eventually gave in? That is capitulating.

This is the heart of the word. The giving-in only counts as capitulation if there was a real struggle before it.

You always capitulate to something — a force, a person, a demand, or pressure of some kind. Common examples:

  • Pressure
  • Demands
  • Threats
  • An opponent or enemy
  • Public opinion
  • Circumstances that leave you no choice
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Capitulating is almost never a happy or willing thing. It carries a strong feeling of reluctance, defeat, or exhaustion. The person who capitulates usually does not want to give in — they do it because:

  • The pressure became too great to bear
  • They ran out of options
  • Continuing to resist felt pointless or impossible
  • They were worn down over time

This is why the word has a slightly heavy, even negative, tone. When you say someone capitulated, you are hinting that they gave up something — their position, their power, their principle — under force or pressure.

In politics:
After weeks of protests outside the parliament, the government finally capitulated and agreed to cancel the new tax.
(The government resisted for weeks, then gave in.)

In everyday life:
She had told her son "no" a dozen times, but after an hour of crying and begging, she capitulated and let him stay up late.
(She held firm repeatedly, then gave in.)

In business:
The company refused to lower its prices for months, but when it started losing customers rapidly, it capitulated to market pressure and cut its rates.
(The company resisted, then gave up its position.)

In an argument:
He had strong views on the topic, but after hearing her evidence, he capitulated and admitted she was right.
(He held his position, then accepted defeat.)

In a historical/military sense:
The fort's soldiers capitulated after a three-month siege, having run out of food and ammunition.
(This is the word's most classic use — a military surrender after a period of holding out.)
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words all involve giving in, but they are not the same:

Surrender — Very close in meaning. But "surrender" can happen immediately (you can surrender the moment someone points a gun at you). Capitulating always requires that you resisted first. Also, "capitulate" often implies that terms or conditions are involved in the giving-in, whereas "surrender" can be total and unconditional.

Give in — Means the same thing in everyday speech, but is very casual and informal. "Capitulate" is the formal, sophisticated version of "give in."

Cave / Cave in — Also means the same thing, but is very informal and slightly slangy. "The boss caved" = "The boss capitulated." Choose "capitulate" in writing or formal speech.

Yield — Milder and more neutral. You can yield graciously, even willingly. Capitulating is more loaded — it almost always suggests reluctance and a harder struggle before the giving-in.

Concede — You concede a specific point in a debate or argument ("I concede that your data is accurate"). Capitulating is bigger — it means giving up your overall position or resistance, not just one point.

Comply — Neutral word, no struggle implied. If you comply with a rule, you simply follow it. If you capitulate to a demand, you fought it before following it.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Capitulate" is a formal word. You will find it in:

  • Newspapers and political reporting
  • History books
  • Business journalism
  • Formal arguments and debates

You would not typically hear it in casual conversation. Someone might say "she finally caved" to a friend, but a journalist would write "she finally capitulated" in an article.

The word almost always appears in these kinds of patterns:

  • capitulate to [something] — He capitulated to the pressure.
  • finally / eventually capitulate — They finally capitulated after months of negotiation.
  • refuse to capitulate — She refused to capitulate, even under intense criticism.
  • capitulate under [pressure/threat] — The regime capitulated under international pressure.

To capitulate means to stop resisting something — after a real struggle — and give in to it, usually reluctantly and under pressure.

If you remember one thing: resistance first, then surrender. That sequence is what "capitulate" is all about.
2504:
Capitulation means the act of giving up resistance and surrendering to someone or something — especially after you have been fighting, struggling, or holding your ground for a significant period of time.

The key word here is after. Capitulation doesn't describe someone who simply agrees to something from the beginning. It describes the moment when a person, a group, an army, or even a market that has been actively resisting finally gives in completely.

Think of it as the breaking point — the moment when resistance collapses.
A Simple Image to Lock It In

Imagine you are in a tug-of-war. You have been pulling hard on the rope for a long time. You're exhausted. The other side is too strong. And then — you let go of the rope entirely.

That letting go is capitulation.

It's not you gently loosening your grip. It's not you negotiating to swap sides. It is a full, complete surrender of your position.
Where and How It Is Used

This word shows up in several different areas of life, and understanding each one will give you a much richer grasp of it.

1. In War and Politics (the most classic use)

When an army or a nation has been defending itself and finally gives up completely — formally laying down arms and accepting the enemy's terms — that is a capitulation. It is a total military or political surrender, and it often carries a sense of defeat and helplessness. The side that capitulates has essentially said: "We cannot fight anymore. We accept your terms."

"The general's capitulation shocked the nation — no one believed the army would surrender so quickly."

This is where the word is most dramatic and weighty.

2. In Everyday Life

You don't need a war to use this word. It applies perfectly to ordinary situations where someone holds out against pressure and then finally gives in — completely.

  • A parent who keeps saying "no" to their child's request for a new phone, but eventually says "fine, take it" out of sheer exhaustion — that is a capitulation.
  • A person who firmly refuses to attend a party but is pestered by friends until they say "okay, I'll come" — that is a capitulation.
  • A politician who publicly opposes a law for months, then votes in favour of it under pressure — that is a capitulation.

In these cases, the word often carries a slight negative or critical tone — suggesting the person should have held their ground but didn't.

3. In Finance and Investing

This is a specific and very important use. In financial markets, capitulation refers to the moment when investors who have been holding on to falling, loss-making investments finally give up and sell everything in panic or despair.

When prices are dropping sharply and investors have been hoping things will turn around, there comes a point where they lose all hope and dump their assets. That mass act of giving up is called capitulation. Interestingly, investors often watch for this moment because it can signal that a market has hit its lowest point — since after everyone who wanted to sell has sold, there's no one left to push prices down further.

"The stock market's capitulation sent share prices to a five-year low before a recovery began."
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Capitulation almost always carries a heavy, slightly negative connotation. It is rarely a neutral or happy word. When you describe something as a capitulation, you are usually suggesting:

  • The person or side gave up when they perhaps should not have, or
  • The surrender was forced upon them by overwhelming pressure, or
  • The giving-in was complete — there was no partial compromise, no dignity saved.

It implies a struggle came before it, and that the struggle ended in defeat for one side.

However, occasionally people use it in a more neutral or even positive sense — as in: "After years of denying the science, the company's capitulation and acceptance of the evidence was a welcome change." Here, the giving-up is seen as the right thing to do, even though the word still signals that a long resistance preceded it.

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as knowing what it is.

Capitulation is not the same as compromise. When two sides compromise, both give something up and both get something in return. It is mutual. Capitulation is one-sided — only one side surrenders, and they surrender entirely.

Capitulation is not the same as simply agreeing. If you agree to something straight away without any resistance, that is just agreement. Capitulation requires that you were against something first, resisted it, and then gave in.

Capitulation is not the same as a concession. A concession is when you give up one specific point while still holding your overall position. Capitulation is the collapse of your entire position — it is total.

Capitulation is not the same as losing. You can lose a battle but still refuse to surrender — still refuse to capitulate. Capitulation is a choice (even if it feels like the only option) to formally stop resisting and accept defeat.

Not all capitulations are equal. The word can describe:

  • A sudden, quick capitulation — where someone folds rapidly under pressure, often seen as a sign of weakness or a lack of genuine conviction.
  • A slow, grinding capitulation — where someone holds on for a long time before finally giving in, often more understandable and sometimes even admirable in retrospect.
  • A total capitulation — where every demand of the opposing side is accepted with nothing gained in return.
  • A partial capitulation — though this use is less common, people sometimes say this to mean someone gave in on most (but not all) points.

Since you will encounter this word's family members too:

  • To capitulate (verb): the action. "She refused to capitulate to their demands."
  • Capitulatory (adjective): relating to or involving capitulation. "His capitulatory tone made it clear he had given up the fight." (Less common, but you may see it.)

Capitulation is the complete, often reluctant act of giving up resistance — surrendering your position, your fight, or your beliefs — after having held out against pressure for a period of time. It applies to wars, politics, everyday life, and financial markets. The word almost always implies that a struggle preceded the giving-in, and it carries a tone of defeat, weakness, or the overwhelming force of circumstances. It is not compromise, not a simple agreement, and not a partial concession — it is a total surrender of the resisting position.
2505: Capoeira is a Brazilian martial art that is uniquely blended with dance, acrobatics, and live music — all at the same time. It is practiced as a kind of "game" between two people, and it looks so graceful and fluid that many people who see it for the first time aren't sure whether they're watching a fight or a performance. The answer is: it is both.

Capoeira is a way of fighting. But unlike boxing or wrestling — where fighters grab, punch, or pin each other — capoeira relies almost entirely on kicks, sweeps, and evasions. A capoeirista (a person who practices capoeira) rarely touches their opponent. Instead, they try to trick the other person, attack from unexpected angles, dodge attacks with fluid body movements, and throw the opponent off balance. The fight is won not by brute force, but by cleverness, agility, and reading the other person's next move.

What makes capoeira especially unusual is that it doesn't look like a fight. The movements are flowing, almost dancing. The two players circle each other in a kind of dialogue — one attacks, the other escapes — and it becomes a beautiful, rhythmic exchange of movement.

In capoeira, a fight is called a jogo, which simply means "game" in Portuguese. This word is important because it captures the spirit of capoeira — it is playful and creative, not brutal or aggressive. Two practitioners enter a circle, read each other's body language, and improvise responses to each other in real time. There are no rounds, no scorecards, no knockouts. The goal is to flow, to outsmart, and to express yourself — while also not getting kicked in the face.

The game can be slow and strategic, almost like a chess match played with bodies, or it can be fast and explosive. Both are valid, and both are deeply skillful.

Capoeira is always practiced inside a roda (pronounced "hoda"), which means "wheel" or "circle." A group of practitioners form a circle, and two people play inside it while the rest watch, clap, and sing. The roda is not just an audience arrangement — it is a sacred space in capoeira culture. Everyone in the circle is participating, even if they are not actively playing. The energy, music, and voices of those in the circle directly influence the game happening inside.

This is where capoeira becomes truly one of a kind. Every session of capoeira is driven by live music, and the music is not background decoration — it is an active part of the game. The rhythm and tempo of the music dictates how the players move. Fast music means a fast, aggressive game. Slow music means a slow, thoughtful, trickery-focused game.

The most important instrument in capoeira is the berimbau — a single-stringed bow with a hollow gourd attached to it, which acts as a resonator. When struck with a stick, it produces a twanging, vibrating sound unlike anything else. It is considered the "voice" of capoeira. Alongside it, practitioners also play the pandeiro (a tambourine), the atabaque (a tall drum), and sometimes other percussion instruments.

Players also sing during the roda. The songs are in Portuguese and carry the history, philosophy, and humor of capoeira. There is usually a ladainha (a solo introductory song), followed by call-and-response singing by the whole group.

The foundation of all capoeira movement is called the ginga (pronounced "jinga"), which means "to sway." It is the constant, swaying side-to-side movement a capoeirista makes when they are not attacking or defending. It is never stillness — a capoeirista in the roda is always moving, always shifting weight, always keeping the opponent unsure of what comes next. The ginga is like the heartbeat of capoeira. It is the first thing a beginner learns and the last thing a master ever stops refining.

Over time, capoeira developed two main branches:

Capoeira Angola is the older, more traditional style. It stays very close to the African roots of the art. The movements tend to be lower to the ground, slower, more deceptive and theatrical. It emphasizes tradition, ritual, and the philosophy behind the art.

Capoeira Regional was created in the 20th century and is more athletic and dynamic. It incorporates higher kicks, more acrobatics, and a faster pace. It is the style most people encounter in modern capoeira schools around the world.

Both styles share the same instruments, the roda, the jogo, and the core philosophy. Many schools today blend elements of both.

In capoeira, the highest title a practitioner can earn is Mestre, which means "master." A Mestre is not just someone who is physically skilled — they are a keeper of tradition, a teacher, a musician, and a living library of capoeira knowledge. Becoming a Mestre typically takes decades of dedication. In capoeira culture, a Mestre is treated with deep respect.

Capoeira was created in Brazil by enslaved Africans, probably beginning in the 16th or 17th century. The enslaved people blended African fighting traditions with music and disguised the martial art within dance so that it would not be immediately recognized as combat training by their captors. Whether this origin story is precisely historical or partly mythological is debated by scholars, but it is central to capoeira's identity and the deep pride practitioners have in it.

For a long time, capoeira was actually illegal in Brazil. It was associated with the poor, the marginalized, and former slaves, and was banned for decades. It only became legal and socially accepted in the 20th century, when it was promoted as a Brazilian cultural treasure.

Today, capoeira is practiced in dozens of countries around the world. In 2014, UNESCO recognized it as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity — a global acknowledgment of its unique value as a living art form.

Capoeira is a Brazilian martial art that is inseparable from music, dance, and culture. It is a game of bodies in conversation — physical, rhythmic, creative, and deeply rooted in a history of resistance and resilience. To practice capoeira is to learn to fight, to dance, to play music, to sing, and to understand a living tradition all at once.
2506:
A caprice is a sudden, unplanned desire, decision, or change of mind that has no strong or logical reason behind it. It comes from a feeling or a mood — not from careful thinking. It is, essentially, a whim.

When someone acts on a caprice, they do something just because they feel like it in that moment — not because it was planned, necessary, or even sensible. The feeling can vanish just as quickly and unexpectedly as it arrived.

Think of it this way: if you walk past an ice cream shop and think, "I wasn't planning on this, I don't even need it, but I just really want some right now" — and you go in — that impulse is a caprice. It is not driven by hunger or logic. It is driven purely by a passing feeling.
The Deeper Essence — What Makes Something a "Caprice"?

Three qualities define a caprice:

Suddenness. It appears without warning. You were not thinking about it a moment ago, and then suddenly you are.

Irrationality. There is no solid, logical reason for it. You simply want it, or you simply feel like doing it.

Unpredictability. Because a caprice is rooted in mood and feeling, it can change just as quickly as it appeared. The desire that felt urgent five minutes ago may completely disappear by the time you act on it.

Together, these three qualities give "caprice" its essential character: it is the will acting without the guidance of reason.
The Tone and Connotation — Is It Positive or Negative?

The word "caprice" sits in an interesting middle space. Depending on context, it can carry a slightly different emotional color.

When used negatively, a caprice suggests unreliability, fickleness, or even irresponsibility. If a king rules by caprice — punishing people based on his mood rather than law — that is dangerous and unfair. If a friend cancels plans every week based on a caprice, they are being inconsiderate. Here, the word implies that someone should be guided by reason or principle, but isn't.

When used neutrally or even warmly, a caprice can describe something charmingly spontaneous, lightly playful, or freely creative — a pleasant surprise without any harm. If a friend shows up at your door unannounced with your favorite food purely on a caprice, it feels delightful rather than reckless. Here, the unpredictability is the very thing that makes the gesture sweet.

So the word itself is not strictly negative. Context determines the tone. What it always carries, however, is the idea of something impulsive and unplanned.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the word working in different ways:

"She moved to Paris on a caprice, with no job lined up and barely any savings."
Here, the caprice is a bold, impulsive life decision with no logical plan behind it — it could be admired as brave or criticized as reckless.

"The children's laughter rose and fell on every caprice of the breeze."
Here, the caprice of the breeze means its random, unpredictable gusts — nature behaving without pattern or purpose.

"He bought the painting not because it matched his home, but as a pure caprice."
A harmless, spontaneous purchase driven by nothing but a passing desire.

"The nobleman's fate depended entirely on the caprice of the king."
Here, "caprice" is clearly negative — the king's arbitrary, mood-driven decisions controlled someone's entire life, which is frightening and unjust.
The Phrase "By Caprice" and "On a Caprice"

You will often see the word used in the phrases "by caprice" or "on a caprice." Both mean as a result of a sudden, unplanned impulse — done for no deeper reason than a passing feeling. These phrases emphasize that no careful thought went into the decision. It just happened because the mood struck.

Because "caprice" is often grouped with words like whim, impulse, and fancy, it helps to understand how they relate.

Whim is the closest synonym and is almost interchangeable with caprice. However, "caprice" tends to feel slightly more literary or formal, and it often implies a stronger, more noticeable degree of unpredictability or unreasonableness than "whim" does.

Impulse suggests speed and instinct — something that happens almost reflexively, before you even have time to think. A caprice is not always that fast; it can be a lingering desire that appeared for no rational reason. The key difference is that "impulse" emphasizes the quickness of the action, while "caprice" emphasizes the lack of reason behind it.

Fancy (as a noun meaning a passing desire) is lighter and softer than caprice. If you have a fancy for strawberries, it is a mild, gentle wish. A caprice tends to imply a greater sense of unpredictability or changeability.

The adjective form of this word — capricious — describes a person or thing that is characterized by caprice. A capricious person is one who changes their mind often, acts on passing moods, and cannot be easily predicted or relied upon. A capricious weather pattern changes frequently and without warning. Knowing this adjective will help you recognize the word's family in your reading.

The word has a well-established life in music and art. A caprice (sometimes written in Italian as capriccio) is a musical composition that is lively, free, and does not follow strict structural rules. The composer writes as the mood takes them — freely, playfully, with creative spontaneity. The most famous examples are the 24 Caprices for solo violin by the Italian composer Paganini — celebrated for their wild, dazzling, and unpredictable character. In visual art, a capriccio is a painting that freely mixes real architectural elements with imaginary ones in a fantastical, invented scene. In both cases, the word in the arts carries a sense of creative freedom liberated from rules — the artist's imagination following its own caprice, going wherever inspiration leads.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you had to compress this word into one sentence: a caprice is a sudden desire or decision driven by feeling and mood, not by logic or reason, and it can disappear just as unpredictably as it arrived. Everything else — the contexts, the tone, the artistic uses — is built on top of that single core idea.
2507:
Capricious describes someone or something that changes suddenly, unpredictably, and without any clear or logical reason — driven purely by impulse or mood.

When you call a person capricious, you're saying they don't follow a stable, predictable pattern. Their decisions, opinions, and moods shift on a whim — not because circumstances changed, not because they thought it through, but simply because they felt like it in that moment. There's no logic you can trace, no reason you can point to. One moment they love something; the next moment they've abandoned it completely.

The key ingredient that makes something capricious isn't just change — it's change without good reason. A doctor who changes their treatment plan because new evidence emerged is not capricious. But a doctor who changes the plan because they woke up in a different mood that morning? That's capricious.

A capricious person is deeply unreliable in a particular way. They might shower you with praise today and be cold and critical tomorrow — not because you did anything differently, but because something shifted inside them. A capricious boss changes project requirements constantly without explanation. A capricious friend cancels plans the moment they feel like doing something else. A capricious ruler rewards loyalty one day and punishes it the next.

The frustrating thing about dealing with a capricious person is that you can never build a reliable model of how they'll behave. Their behavior seems almost random — but not because they're complex. It's because they're governed by passing feelings rather than steady principles.
In things, nature, and abstract ideas

Capricious isn't only used for people. It's applied to anything that behaves with sudden, unexplained inconsistency.

Weather is one of the most common examples. "Capricious spring weather" means weather that is gloriously sunny one hour and stormy the next — not following any pattern you can prepare for. The sea can be capricious. Fate can be capricious. Markets, policies, and even artistic inspiration are described this way. When something is beyond your control and changes wildly for no clear reason, "capricious" fits perfectly.

Capricious is almost always a negative or critical word. Calling someone capricious implies they are unreliable, unstable, and difficult to trust or deal with. It suggests a lack of seriousness and principled thinking. Nobody wants to be called capricious — it paints you as someone whose word means little, because your feelings tomorrow might erase your commitments today.

There is one exception: in creative or artistic contexts, the word can occasionally be used with mild admiration. "A capricious imagination" might mean a creative mind that leaps freely and unpredictably from one idea to another, which in that specific setting can feel freeing rather than frustrating. But outside of art and creativity, assume the word carries criticism.
How it differs from similar words

Several words are close neighbors of capricious, and knowing the differences makes your understanding sharper.

Fickle is the closest synonym. Both words describe unpredictable change driven by mood rather than reason. But "fickle" tends to be used specifically about emotional loyalty — you might call a romantic partner fickle, or sports fans fickle. "Capricious" is broader and slightly more formal, used comfortably for people, nature, fate, and systems alike.

Impulsive means acting quickly without thinking. It describes a single moment — one rushed decision made without deliberation. Capricious, on the other hand, describes a long-term pattern of behavior. An impulsive person made one hasty choice; a capricious person has a whole lifestyle of inconsistency.

Erratic means irregular and unpredictable, but it doesn't necessarily carry the "whim" quality. Erratic behavior might be caused by external pressures, stress, or illness. Capricious specifically implies the change comes from within — from mood, fancy, or impulse — rather than from outside forces.

Mercurial is very similar to capricious and is sometimes used interchangeably. The subtle difference is that mercurial tends to emphasize rapid shifts specifically in mood, while capricious is broader, covering changes in opinion, decision, behavior, and judgment as well.

Whimsical looks similar in concept but is almost the opposite in feeling. Whimsical means playfully imaginative and fanciful — it's charming and lighthearted. Capricious is the serious, critical version of the same energy. A children's storybook can be whimsical; a CEO making random policy changes is capricious.

"The capricious king could sentence you to prison or reward you with a palace on the same afternoon — nobody around him ever felt safe."

"She left the job because her manager was capricious, changing the project goals every few days without explanation or apology."

"The capricious mountain weather caught the hikers off guard — clear skies turned into heavy snow in under an hour."

"Investors were frustrated by the capricious new regulations, which seemed to shift direction every month."

"Even as a young child, he was capricious — fiercely devoted to a hobby for a week, then completely indifferent to it by the next."

Here are the other forms briefly so you have the complete picture. The adverb is capriciously ("she capriciously changed her mind again"). The noun is capriciousness ("his capriciousness made him impossible to work with") or, more elegantly, caprice ("she acted on a caprice" — meaning she acted on a whim).
A simple mental image to lock it in forever

Picture someone spinning a wheel of fortune to decide every choice in their life — what they believe, who they like, what they want, how they feel — and then spinning it again an hour later just because they can. That's a capricious person. No pattern, no reason, no warning. Just whim, ruling everything.
2508:
To capsize means to overturn a boat or other watercraft in water — that is, to flip it upside down or onto its side so that the bottom faces up and the deck faces down (or sideways).

This is different from simply sinking (going underwater). A capsized vessel often still floats — just upside down. It has been flipped, not necessarily swallowed by the sea.

"Capsize" works in two ways:

1. Without an object (intransitive) — the vessel overturns by itself:

The small boat capsized in the storm.
The canoe capsized when he leaned too far to one side.

Here, something causes it — waves, wind, imbalance — but grammatically, the boat is the subject doing the capsizing.

2. With an object (transitive) — something causes the vessel to overturn:

The giant wave capsized the fishing boat.
Strong winds capsized several yachts during the race.

Here, the wave or wind is the agent; the boat is the thing being flipped.
What Exactly Happens When Something Capsizes

Picture a kayak floating upright on a lake. Now imagine a wave hits it hard from the side. The kayak rolls over — its flat bottom is now pointing at the sky, and the cockpit (where the paddler sits) is now underwater. The kayak has capsized. The paddler has likely been thrown into the water.

The key visual: the vessel is no longer in its normal, upright, usable position. It has been overturned.

The word is used most naturally with watercraft of all sizes:

  • A canoe, a kayak, a dinghy (small rowboat), a sailboat, a yacht, a ferry, or even a large ship — all of these can capsize.

The bigger the vessel, the more dramatic (and dangerous) the capsizing.

• Rough weather — storms, strong winds, high waves
  • Imbalance — too much weight on one side, passengers moving suddenly to one side
  • Collision — hitting a rock, reef, or another vessel
  • Human error — poor steering, overloading, going too fast in rough water

Like many vivid physical words, "capsize" is sometimes used metaphorically to describe something being completely overturned, destabilized, or ruined:

The financial scandal capsized the entire company.
One bad decision capsized his career.

This use borrows the image of sudden, catastrophic overturning and applies it to abstract things — plans, organizations, careers, governments. It suggests not just damage, but a total loss of stability and normal functioning.

This figurative use is less common than the literal one, but you will encounter it in journalism and literary writing.

• Sink — to go under the water and disappear beneath the surface. A boat can capsize without sinking (it floats upside down). Or it can capsize and then sink.
  • Overturn — a broader word meaning to flip something upside down. It works for boats, cars, and other objects. "Capsize" is the specific, precise word reserved almost exclusively for watercraft.
  • Keel over — an informal, idiomatic phrase that means roughly the same thing as capsize when used about boats. It can also mean a person fainting or falling over suddenly.
  • Tip over — very casual; used for small boats or objects. A cup can "tip over"; a tanker ship would "capsize," not "tip over."

To capsize is to overturn a boat or vessel in water so it flips upside down or onto its side — whether by the force of weather, waves, imbalance, or collision — and by extension, to completely destabilize or ruin something.
2509: A capsule is a small, self-contained shell or container that encloses something inside it — protecting it, preserving it, or keeping it neatly packaged. Think of it as a tight little "wrapper" around something. This core idea of enclosing something inside a compact shell runs through every use of this word.

1. A medicine capsule
This is the most everyday use. A capsule is a small, smooth, oval-shaped container — usually made of a thin layer of gelatin (a soft, dissolvable material) — that holds medicine (powder, liquid, or small granules) inside it. You swallow it like a pill. Once it reaches your stomach, the outer shell dissolves and releases the medicine inside.

This is different from a tablet (which is medicine pressed into a solid shape) because a capsule is hollow on the inside and carries something within its shell.

"Take one capsule twice a day with water."

2. A space capsule
In aerospace, a capsule is the small, sealed cabin — usually shaped like a cone or a pod — at the top of a rocket or spacecraft, where astronauts sit and live during a mission. It is designed to survive extreme conditions (the vacuum of space, intense heat during re-entry into Earth's atmosphere) and keep the people inside safe and alive.

"The astronauts splashed down in the ocean inside the capsule."

3. A time capsule
A time capsule is a sealed container in which people place objects, letters, photographs, or other items that represent their current time and life — and then bury it or store it away to be opened years or decades later. The idea is to "capture" a moment in time and preserve it for the future.

"The school buried a time capsule containing newspapers and drawings, to be opened in 50 years."

4. A biological/anatomical capsule
In science and medicine, a capsule refers to a thin, membrane-like covering or sac that surrounds and protects an organ or a body part.

  • Your knee joint has a joint capsule — a tough fibrous bag that wraps around the joint, holds the joint fluid in, and keeps the bones in place.
  • Your kidneys have a renal capsule — a thin protective layer on the outside of each kidney.
  • Many bacteria have a polysaccharide capsule — a slimy outer coating that protects them from the body's immune system.

In all these cases, the capsule is nature's version of a protective shell.

5. A botanical capsule (plant biology)
In botany, a capsule is a type of dry fruit or seed pod that contains seeds inside. When the seeds are ripe and ready to be dispersed, the capsule dries out and splits open (or develops small holes) to release them.

Common examples: poppy seed pods, cotton bolls (before they burst open with fluffy cotton), and the seed pods of certain flowers like snapdragons.

Once you understand that a capsule means "a compact, self-contained unit that holds something," you'll see the word used figuratively too.

Capsule wardrobe
A "capsule wardrobe" is a small, carefully chosen collection of clothing — usually only essential, versatile, high-quality pieces — that can be mixed and matched to create many different outfits. The idea is that these few items "contain" everything you need, just like a capsule contains medicine.

"She built a capsule wardrobe of 30 items that covered every occasion."

Capsule summary / capsule review / capsule biography
When the word "capsule" is used before a noun like this, it means brief and self-contained — a short version that packs all the key information into a small space, like a capsule packs medicine into a shell.

"The magazine published a capsule review of each film — just two sentences, capturing the essential point."
"Here is a capsule biography of the author." (meaning a very short, condensed biography)

Whenever you see the word "capsule," ask yourself: what is being enclosed, protected, or compactly packaged here?

  • Medicine capsule → medicine enclosed in a gelatin shell
  • Space capsule → astronauts enclosed in a protective pod
  • Time capsule → memories enclosed in a sealed container for the future
  • Joint capsule → a joint enclosed in a protective biological sac
  • Seed capsule → seeds enclosed in a plant pod
  • Capsule wardrobe → a complete wardrobe enclosed in just a few items
  • Capsule review → a complete review enclosed in just a few words

The thread connecting all of these is the same: something complete and useful, packed tightly inside a small, enclosed unit.

A capsule is a small, enclosed container or shell that holds something inside it — often to protect it, preserve it, or keep it neatly contained. The object inside could be medicine, a person (in space), seeds (in a plant), or even an idea (in writing). When used figuratively, it describes anything that is compact, self-contained, and complete in a small form.
